claims.text: The stress–strain and thermoelastic behaviors of HfNbTaTiZr arise from residual stresses generated by thermal-expansion mismatch among microstructural constituents.
Thermally induced residual stresses modulate dislocation mobility and recovery.
Internal residual stresses govern the high-temperature tensile-creep behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
Internal residual stresses govern microhardness changes during cold work in HfNbTaTiZr.
Internal residual stresses govern temperature-dependent elastic-modulus changes in HfNbTaTiZr.
As-processed HfNbTaTiZr has a random solid-solution microstructure.
Slight compositional or grain-boundary heterogeneities in HfNbTaTiZr predispose the alloy to differential thermal expansion.
A stress-relief anneal reduces thermal-mismatch residual stresses relative to the standard processing cycle.
The relevant elastic-modulus behavior occurs from approximately 293 to 1100 K.
HfNbTaTiZr undergoes aging-induced hardening in the 600–800 °C range.
The relevant tensile-creep behavior of HfNbTaTiZr occurs around 1250 °C.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between grains or incipient precipitates creates localized stress fields.
Localized mismatch-induced stress fields influence dislocation activation, creep mechanisms, and elastic response.
Differential thermal expansion during cooling and thermal cycling creates internal residual stresses.
Residual stresses alter local energy barriers for dislocation motion.
Samples retaining more residual thermoelastic mismatch will have higher post-cold-work microhardness than stress-relieved samples.
Samples retaining more residual thermoelastic mismatch will have higher elevated-temperature elastic moduli than stress-relieved samples.
Samples retaining more residual thermoelastic mismatch will have lower tensile-creep rates than stress-relieved samples.
Stress-relieved samples will show a more uniform and predictable mechanical response.
Earlier creep, aging, and elastic-modulus observations support a residual-stress mechanism in HfNbTaTiZr.
